title: Something is rotten in the state of Denmark
subtitle: 6 Things I've Learned About Denmark
html:
I’m on a train in Denmark, sitting in the Stillezone (Quite zone). Before arriving a week ago, I had a romanticized view of Scandinavia: clean, safe, free college and healthcare, amazing infrastructure… the list goes on. I also befriended an old (96 years old now) Danish man who, through his rose-colored glasses tinted with nostalgia, told me his views about the Danish people and their culture. He made a compelling case that I ought to experience it for myself. So, after finishing my master’s degree just two weeks ago (December 2025, at the time of writing this), I set off to see what all the hype was about. After over a week of galavanting, staring into the Baltic Sea, and making approximately zero eye contact with Danes in the streets, I figured now would be an appropriate time to reflect on my adventure so far and share some of my takeaways.

1. Eye contact

My first observation after deplaning in Copenhagen was that the Danes resemble Americans of the northeast in that they seldom make eye contact with you or acknowledge your existence in public. If you’re walking alone, boy, you will feel alone. No smiles, no nods, no warmth. As a midwesterner with “Minnesota Nice” coursing through his veins, this was an unpleasant shock.

2. Beauty: Maybe there’s something in the water over here, but my god. I’ve been genuinely startled by the beauty of some of the Danes. The woman working the front desk at a gym I trained at looked like the output of ChatGPT if asked, “generate an image of the most beautiful woman imaginable with blonde hair and blue eyes.” And this isn’t just hyperbole. I ran the test. I generated the image. The resemblance is uncanny. Needless to say, I was a bit distracted during my workout. What’s crazier is that these people are everywhere. Men and women here are, on average, significantly more attractive than anywhere else I’ve been. See below for the ChatGPT image.

3. Egalitarianism

Danish culture is very egalitarian. The idea of a man paying on a first date, or of walking a woman home to make sure she gets back safely, would seem strange to Danes. They’re independent and equal. At least, they are in the minds of the Danes. Why would a woman need a man to do anything for her?

In talking with some Danes and some expats living in Denmark, there’s no reason to believe that this is the ideal. It might be for some, but it’s also true that some women dream of becoming stay-at-home moms—living in partnership with a competent provider. And there’s no wrong answer! What makes the most sense to me is that we shouldn’t optimize for equality, whatever that even means. Rather, we should optimize for freedom. Ensuring that men and women are free to be and do what they want, and free to create the relationship dynamic that works best for them. There is no need to impose your optimal solution on others whose optimal solution may differ.

4. Interior Design

The Danes are famous for their interior design. Inside spaces are pretty here. There’s the perfect amount of furniture, decoration, and color. My time here made me realize just how beautiful a blank wall could be when in the right context. Sometimes, the best thing to do is less.

5. American Stereotypes

From my limited sample size, Danes seem to think Americans are loud, dumb, friendly, and fake. Fair enough 🤷‍♂️.

6. Booze and Bistability

One of the most bewildering things I noticed about the Danes is that they have a kind of bistability—two equilibrium states they exist in that are mutually exclusive. Either they’re sober and closed, as I observed immediately after arriving here, or they’re drunk and communal.

I went out to a couple of clubs last night with an expat from the States. I didn’t drink. I just observed. And what I saw was remarkable. Not remarkable compared to any other club or bar environment, but remarkable compared to the Danes’ default setting. The cold, closed-off, independent Danes were sitting at tables, with friends and with strangers, shouting, laughing, and stumbling around. They were warm and friendly! I met a nice Danish man named Julius, who I’m pretty sure was trying to steal my date, and a random guy at the bar who asked if I was American because I had “a very American phenotype.” I even got several compliments on my physique (exclusively from men, of course). Did I enjoy myself at the clubs? No, not particularly😂🤷‍♂️. But I had some rich new experiences, and I’d consider that a win.

Overall, my trip to Denmark has taught me that, above all, people are people, no matter where you are. They do what they’re conditioned and predisposed to do, whether that be to stare blankly into space as you pass them on the sidewalk, or to draw dicks in the frost on public benches.

It’s a beautiful place with beautiful people, and I intend to return someday.
